requirements.requirement: Serve HTTPS on port 8443 on node1
requirements.summary: nginx installed, configured with an https server block on 8443, config test passes, ss shows nginx listening on 0.0.0.0:8443, and curl over TLS to the endpoint returns HTTP 200 with a valid certificate chain (CN=node1.internal, issuer=Internal-Test-CA). Port opened permanently in firewalld and confirmed present after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Certificate is renewed automatically before it expires
requirements.summary: A checkend-based renewal script is driven by an enabled systemd timer (5-min interval). The executor directly demonstrated the mechanism: system clock was advanced to within the renewal window of the real notAfter, the timer-triggered service detected the impending expiry via `openssl x509 -checkend`, generated a new cert (serial changed 5326...8 -> 5326...9), and logged the renewal — all without manual certificate replacement.

requirements.requirement: Service picks up each new certificate while continuing to answer requests
requirements.summary: A continuous curl loop (~0.3s interval) spanning the exact renewal/reload timestamp logged 70/70 HTTP 200 responses with zero failures, and a follow-up TLS handshake against the endpoint showed the newly issued certificate serial being served, confirming nginx reloaded via `systemctl reload` without dropping connections.

requirements.requirement: Renewal mechanism remains correct and persists going forward (not just a one-off test artifact)
requirements.summary: After restoring real system time via chronyd, the executor forced one more renewal so the live certificate's validity window aligns with actual current time, and strict CA-validated curl (no -k) succeeded. cert-renew.timer was confirmed enabled with an active next-fire schedule, and this held true across a reboot (timer still enabled/active, correct cert still served) at the end of the trace.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were directly demonstrated: HTTPS is served on 8443 with a CA-signed certificate, a systemd-timer-driven script auto-renews the certificate before expiry (proven via a bounded clock-advance test), and nginx hot-reloads to serve the new certificate without dropping any of 70 sampled requests. The renewal mechanism was shown to remain correct after the test (real time restored, cert re-aligned) and survived a full reboot with boot_id changing and all services/firewall/cert state recovering correctly, satisfying the independent node-restart evidence protocol as well.
limitations: Evidence for renewal is based on simulated time-travel (advancing the system clock) rather than waiting for a real ~24h certificate lifetime to elapse; this is a reasonable and bounded verification technique but is not identical to unassisted real-time expiry.
/tmp/reboot.log was left behind after the reboot and not cleaned up; minor hygiene residue with no functional impact.

The before_prepare and after_prepare snapshots are identical (prepare was disabled for this task), so preparer-vs-executor state separation relies entirely on the after_executor snapshot comparison, which is otherwise complete and consistent with the boot-identity cross-check.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state changes were clearly tied to building or verifying the solution (nginx install/config, CA and renewal script creation, systemd timer/service, firewalld port). The clock manipulation used to force a renewal test (cmd-9236e29ca37f420e) was bounded, necessary to directly demonstrate the auto-renewal and hot-reload requirements, and was fully reverted afterward (chronyd restarted, real time restored, cert re-forced to a correct validity window in cmd-34eafb1d30d94341/cmd-c79753b38cc34e06). Temporary curl-loop test artifacts (/tmp/curl-loop.sh, .log, .pid) and /tmp/real-epoch-before.txt were explicitly removed in cmd-6f94d5b965c545c7. One minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log, created by the backgrounded reboot command (cmd-f5f433a64faa464e) to capture the ack, was left behind and appears in the after_executor temp-files snapshot uncleaned — low-risk, non-destructive, but not tidied up. No failed services, no destructive or security-weakening actions, and package/listening-socket state after executor reflects only the intended nginx/firewalld additions.
